question: A payments company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances that must decrypt and process cardholder data. Security policy requires that the decryption step runs in a hardened, isolated environment that has no persistent storage, no interactive access, and no external network connectivity, even for administrators of the parent instance. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Run the decryption code in an AWS Nitro Enclave created from the parent EC2 instance and use cryptographic attestation with AWS KMS
Launch the decryption code on a Dedicated Host so that no other AWS customer shares the physical server
Run the decryption code in a separate Docker container on the same instance with a restrictive seccomp profile
Move the decryption code to an instance in a private subnet with a security group that denies all inbound traffic
explanation: Nitro Enclaves carve isolated CPU and memory out of the parent instance into an environment with no persistent storage, no interactive access, and no external networking; only a local vsock channel to the parent exists, and AWS KMS can verify the enclave through attestation. A Dedicated Host isolates hardware from other customers but does not isolate data from administrators of the instance. A container shares the kernel and is reachable by instance administrators. A private subnet limits network paths but still allows interactive access and persistent storage.

question: Which statement BEST explains why EC2 instances built on the AWS Nitro System deliver performance close to bare metal?
options: Each Nitro-based instance is always placed on a Dedicated Host so that it never shares physical hardware with other instances
The Nitro hypervisor emulates every hardware device in software, which removes the need for device drivers in the guest operating system
Nitro-based instances store all data on local instance store volumes instead of network-attached EBS volumes
Networking, EBS storage, and management functions are offloaded to dedicated Nitro cards, and a lightweight hypervisor leaves nearly all host CPU and memory to the instance
explanation: The Nitro System moves virtualization functions such as VPC networking, EBS access, and instance management onto purpose-built Nitro cards and uses a minimal hypervisor, so almost all host resources go to the workload. Nitro-based instances use shared tenancy by default rather than Dedicated Hosts. Full software device emulation is the slower approach that Nitro replaced. Nitro-based instances commonly use EBS, and instance store is available only on certain instance types.

question: A company runs its customer portal on a single EC2 instance in one Availability Zone. An outage in that Availability Zone made the portal unavailable for several hours. The company wants the portal to remain available if an entire Availability Zone fails. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Place the instance in a spread placement group so that it runs on distinct hardware racks
Run the application in an Auto Scaling group that spans subnets in at least two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer
Replace the instance with a larger instance type that has more vCPUs and enable termination protection
Associate an Elastic IP address with the instance so that it can be moved quickly during an outage
explanation: An EC2 instance runs in one subnet and therefore in one Availability Zone, so surviving an AZ failure requires instances in multiple AZs, a load balancer to route around the failed AZ, and an Auto Scaling group to replace capacity. A larger instance is still a single point of failure in one AZ. An Elastic IP address does not create capacity in a second AZ. A spread placement group separates racks, but a single instance still lives in a single AZ.

question: A company must relocate an EC2 instance and its 2 TiB EBS data volume from us-east-1a to us-east-1c in the same Region so that it is closer to new database replicas. Which approach will accomplish this?
options: Detach the EBS volume and attach it to a new instance launched in us-east-1c
Modify the instance placement attribute to us-east-1c and then start the instance
Create an AMI and EBS snapshots, then launch a new instance from the AMI and create the data volume from the snapshot in us-east-1c
Enable EBS Multi-Attach so that the volume can be attached to instances in both Availability Zones
explanation: EBS volumes are bound to the Availability Zone in which they were created, and an existing instance cannot change its AZ. Snapshots and AMIs are Regional, so they can be used to create a new instance and new volumes in any AZ of the Region. A volume cannot be attached to an instance in a different AZ, and Multi-Attach only works for instances in the same AZ.

question: A company is migrating a self-managed in-memory analytics database that needs 512 GiB of RAM but only moderate CPU. Which EC2 instance family is the MOST appropriate starting point?
options: Memory optimized (R family)
Storage optimized (I family)
Accelerated computing (G family)
Compute optimized (C family)
explanation: Memory optimized R instances provide a high memory-to-vCPU ratio, which suits in-memory databases and real-time analytics. Compute optimized C instances would require paying for many unneeded vCPUs to reach 512 GiB of memory. Storage optimized I instances focus on fast local NVMe storage, and G instances provide GPUs for graphics and inference workloads.

question: A company runs a reporting service on a t3.xlarge instance in standard credit mode. CloudWatch shows the instance has averaged 75% CPU utilization all day, every day, for 3 months, and the CPU credit balance stays at zero, which makes reports slow. Which change will resolve the performance problem MOST cost-effectively?
options: Change to a t3.2xlarge instance in standard credit mode so that it earns credits faster
Add a second t3.xlarge instance behind a load balancer to share the load
Change to a fixed-performance general purpose instance, such as an M-family instance of similar size
Switch the instance to unlimited credit mode and keep the t3.xlarge instance type
explanation: Burstable T instances are cost-effective only when average CPU stays below the baseline, and a sustained 75% load is far above the t3.xlarge baseline, so a fixed-performance M instance delivers full CPU at a predictable lower price. Unlimited mode removes throttling but continuously charges for surplus credits, which typically costs more than an equivalent M instance at this utilization. Moving to a t3.2xlarge or adding a second T instance roughly doubles the hourly cost to buy headroom that a same-sized M instance provides natively.

question: A genomics company runs a sequence-alignment pipeline that reads and writes millions of small temporary files and needs very high random IOPS with very low latency to local storage. The intermediate files can be regenerated if they are lost. Which instance choice is MOST suitable?
options: A memory optimized R instance with a gp3 volume provisioned at the baseline 3,000 IOPS
A compute optimized C instance with an st1 Throughput Optimized HDD volume
A general purpose M instance with several sc1 Cold HDD volumes striped in RAID 0
A storage optimized instance, such as I4i, that provides local NVMe SSD instance store volumes
explanation: Storage optimized I-family instances include local NVMe instance store that delivers very high random IOPS at very low latency, and the risk of data loss is acceptable because the files can be regenerated. A gp3 volume at baseline offers only 3,000 IOPS over the network. st1 and sc1 are HDD volume types designed for large sequential I/O, not small random I/O.

question: A company wants developers to open SSH sessions to Amazon Linux 2023 instances without distributing or rotating long-lived SSH private keys. Access must be granted and revoked through IAM policies, and every connection request must be recorded in AWS CloudTrail. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Store a shared private key in AWS Secrets Manager and let developers retrieve it when they need access
Use EC2 Instance Connect so that IAM-authorized users push a short-lived public key to the instance for each session
Create a separate EC2 key pair for each developer and add all of the public keys to authorized_keys through user data
Deploy a bastion host in a public subnet and require developers to use SSH agent forwarding through it
explanation: EC2 Instance Connect uses IAM to authorize the SendSSHPublicKey API, which places a one-time public key on the instance that is valid for 60 seconds, and these API calls are logged in CloudTrail. A shared key in Secrets Manager is still a long-lived credential that must be rotated. Per-developer key pairs require distribution and cleanup. A bastion host adds infrastructure and still relies on long-lived keys.

question: An administrator tries to connect to an EC2 instance in a public subnet by using the browser-based EC2 Instance Connect option in the console, but the connection fails. The instance has a public IPv4 address, the EC2 Instance Connect package is installed, and the security group allows inbound TCP port 22 only from the corporate office CIDR range. What should the administrator do to allow console connections while keeping SSH restricted?
options: Update the network ACL to allow inbound ephemeral ports from the corporate office CIDR range
Add an inbound rule for TCP port 22 from the AWS-managed EC2 Instance Connect prefix list for the Region
Add an outbound rule for TCP port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 in the instance security group
Attach an instance profile to the instance that allows ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey
explanation: Browser-based EC2 Instance Connect sessions originate from the EC2 Instance Connect service IP range, not from the administrator's office, so the security group must allow port 22 from that range, which AWS publishes as a managed prefix list in each Region. Security groups are stateful, so an outbound rule is not the issue. The SendSSHPublicKey permission is needed by the IAM principal making the request, not by the instance. Changing the network ACL for the office range does not admit traffic from the service range.

question: A company has EC2 instances in private subnets with no public IP addresses and no route to an internet gateway. Administrators occasionally need SSH access from the AWS Management Console or the AWS CLI. The company wants to avoid running and patching bastion hosts. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint in the VPC and allow SSH from the endpoint's security group to the instances
Create a VPC peering connection to a management VPC that hosts a single bastion host
Associate Elastic IP addresses with the instances and restrict the security group to administrator IP addresses
Deploy a NAT gateway so that administrators can connect through it to the private instances
explanation: An EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint provides IAM-authenticated SSH and RDP connectivity to instances in private subnets without public IP addresses, internet gateways, or bastion hosts. Elastic IP addresses would expose the instances publicly. A NAT gateway only supports connections initiated from inside the private subnet. A bastion host in a peered VPC is still a bastion host that must be operated and patched.

question: A company runs a clustered application on four Nitro-based EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone. The application uses a cluster-aware file system and requires all four instances to have concurrent read and write access to the same low-latency block storage volume. Which storage option meets these requirements?
options: An st1 volume with Multi-Attach enabled
Instance store volumes on each instance that are synchronized with rsync
A Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume with Multi-Attach enabled
A gp3 volume attached to one instance and exported to the other instances over NFS
explanation: Multi-Attach lets a single io1 or io2 volume be attached to up to 16 Nitro-based instances in the same Availability Zone, and a cluster-aware file system coordinates concurrent writes. gp3 volumes do not support Multi-Attach, and exporting a volume over NFS adds a single point of failure and extra latency. st1 volumes do not support Multi-Attach. Instance store volumes are separate per instance, and rsync does not provide shared concurrent block access.

question: A company runs a database on a 2,000 GiB gp2 volume. The data set is only 400 GiB, but the team provisioned the large volume to obtain 6,000 IOPS. Peak throughput is 200 MiB/s. The company wants to reduce EBS costs without reducing performance. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective?
options: Change the existing volume to st1 to take advantage of lower per-GiB pricing
Keep gp2 and add a second 400 GiB gp2 volume configured in RAID 0
Create a new 400 GiB io2 volume provisioned with 6,000 IOPS and migrate the data
Create a new 400 GiB gp3 volume provisioned with 6,000 IOPS and 200 MiB/s of throughput, and migrate the data
explanation: gp2 performance scales at 3 IOPS per GiB, which is why the volume was oversized, while gp3 lets IOPS and throughput be provisioned independently of size at a lower per-GiB price. A 400 GiB gp3 volume with 6,000 IOPS and 200 MiB/s therefore meets the need at the lowest cost; because EBS volumes cannot be shrunk, a new volume and a data migration are required. io2 provides the IOPS at a much higher price. st1 is HDD-based and unsuitable for random database I/O, and two 400 GiB gp2 volumes provide only about 2,400 baseline IOPS.

question: A financial services company is moving a mission-critical relational database to EC2. The database requires 200,000 sustained IOPS on a single volume, consistent sub-millisecond latency, and the highest durability that EBS offers. Which EBS volume type should a solutions architect choose?
options: General Purpose SSD (gp3) with the maximum provisioned IOPS
Provisioned IOPS SSD io2 Block Express
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1) on a Xen-based instance
explanation: io2 Block Express supports up to 256,000 IOPS per volume with sub-millisecond latency and is designed for 99.999% durability, the highest of any EBS volume type. gp3 cannot reach 200,000 IOPS on a single volume and has lower durability. st1 is an HDD type intended for sequential throughput. io1 has lower durability and a maximum IOPS far below 200,000, especially on older Xen-based instances.

question: A media analytics company processes 12 TiB of clickstream logs every night with a Hadoop job that reads files sequentially in large blocks. The data must stay on EBS. The company wants the lowest-cost volume type that still provides high sequential throughput for this frequently accessed data. Which volume type should be used?
options: Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2)
General Purpose SSD (gp3)
Cold HDD (sc1)
explanation: st1 is a low-cost HDD volume type designed for frequently accessed, throughput-intensive sequential workloads such as big data, data warehouses, and log processing. io2 and gp3 are SSD types optimized for IOPS and cost more per GiB for this amount of data. sc1 is cheaper but is intended for infrequently accessed data and offers much lower throughput, which would slow the nightly job.

question: A company must keep 30 TiB of rarely accessed archive data on block storage attached to an EC2 instance for a legacy application. The data is read only a few times a year in large sequential scans. Which EBS volume type is the MOST cost-effective?
options: Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
General Purpose SSD (gp2)
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1)
Cold HDD (sc1)
explanation: sc1 has the lowest cost per GiB of the EBS volume types and is designed for large, infrequently accessed, sequential workloads. st1 is designed for frequently accessed, throughput-heavy data and costs more. The SSD types are priced for IOPS-sensitive workloads and would be the most expensive way to store cold data.

question: A solutions architect is creating a launch template and must choose the EBS volume type for the root (boot) volume of the instances. Which EBS volume types can be used as a boot volume? (Select TWO.)
options: Cold HDD (sc1)
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2)
General Purpose SSD (gp3)
Any HDD volume type, as long as Fast Snapshot Restore is enabled on its snapshot
explanation: SSD-backed volume types such as gp3 and io2 can be used as boot volumes. The HDD-backed st1 and sc1 volume types cannot be boot volumes regardless of size, and Fast Snapshot Restore only affects how quickly a restored volume reaches full performance, not whether a volume type is bootable.

question: A company runs a fleet of web servers that each keep a large local cache of rendered page fragments. The cache can be rebuilt from the origin database at any time, and the company wants the lowest possible read latency for the cache with no additional storage charges. Which storage option should the company use for the cache?
options: An Amazon EFS file system mounted on all of the web servers
An EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach enabled
Instance store volumes on an instance type that includes local NVMe storage
An EBS gp3 volume with additional provisioned throughput
explanation: Instance store volumes are physically attached to the host, provide very low latency and high IOPS, and are included in the instance price, which suits a cache that can be rebuilt if the instance stops or fails. gp3 and io2 volumes are network-attached and billed separately. EFS adds network latency and per-GB charges and is designed for shared file access rather than a per-instance cache.

question: An application writes temporary data to instance store volumes on an EC2 instance. Which actions will cause the data on the instance store volumes to be lost? (Select TWO.)
options: Changing the security groups attached to the instance
Creating an EBS snapshot of the root volume
Stopping the instance
Terminating the instance
Rebooting the instance from the operating system
explanation: Instance store is ephemeral storage tied to the physical host, so its data is lost when the instance is stopped, hibernated, or terminated, or when the underlying hardware fails. A reboot keeps the instance on the same host, so instance store data persists. Snapshotting an EBS volume and changing security groups do not affect instance store data.

question: A company needs daily snapshots of the EBS volumes attached to production EC2 instances that are tagged Env=prod. Snapshots must be kept for 14 days and copied automatically to a second Region for disaster recovery. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on each volume in both Regions
Write a Lambda function that calls CreateSnapshot and CopySnapshot, and invoke it on an Amazon EventBridge schedule
Create an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy that targets the tag, retains 14 daily snapshots, and enables cross-Region copy
Configure a cron job on each instance that runs AWS CLI commands to create and copy snapshots
explanation: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager natively creates snapshots for tagged resources on a schedule, enforces retention, and copies snapshots to other Regions without custom code. A Lambda function or cron jobs can work but require code, error handling, and retention cleanup to be maintained. Fast Snapshot Restore speeds up volume initialization and does not create or copy snapshots.

question: A company restores EBS volumes from snapshots every morning to launch analytics instances before a trading window opens. Immediately after the restore, the first reads from each block are slow, which delays the start of the job. The company needs restored volumes to deliver their full provisioned performance immediately. What should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Enable Fast Snapshot Restore for the snapshots in the Availability Zones where the volumes are created
Create the volumes as io2 Block Express volumes instead of gp3 volumes
Move the snapshots to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier
Increase the provisioned IOPS of the volumes after they are created
explanation: Volumes created from snapshots are lazily loaded from Amazon S3, so the first access to each block incurs extra latency; Fast Snapshot Restore creates volumes that are fully initialized in the enabled Availability Zones, so they deliver full performance immediately. The archive tier is for low-cost long-term retention and makes restores slower. Increasing IOPS or choosing io2 does not remove the first-read penalty of lazy loading.

question: Once a month, a company restores a 1 TiB EBS volume from a snapshot for a batch job that starts 8 hours after the volume is created. The first reads are slow because of volume initialization. The company wants full performance when the job starts and wants to minimize cost. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on the snapshot permanently in the target Availability Zone
Initialize the volume after it is created by reading all of its blocks with a tool such as fio or dd before the job starts
Restore the snapshot to an io2 volume with the highest possible provisioned IOPS
Move the snapshot to the archive tier and restore it a day in advance
explanation: Reading every block after creation forces all data to be pulled from Amazon S3, and with 8 hours available the volume will be fully initialized before the job starts at no additional charge. Fast Snapshot Restore is billed for every hour it is enabled per snapshot and Availability Zone, which is wasteful for a monthly job. A high-IOPS io2 volume still suffers from lazy loading and costs more. Archived snapshots take much longer to restore and still require initialization.

question: A company must retain monthly EBS snapshots of its accounting servers for 7 years for audit purposes. The snapshots are almost never restored, and a restore time of up to 72 hours is acceptable. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective?
options: Keep the snapshots in the standard snapshot tier and enable Recycle Bin
Copy the snapshots to a second Region and delete the originals
Create AMIs from the snapshots and then deregister the AMIs
Move the snapshots to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier
explanation: EBS Snapshots Archive stores full snapshots at up to 75% lower cost than the standard tier and is intended for rarely accessed snapshots kept for 90 days or longer, with restores completing within 72 hours. Recycle Bin protects against accidental deletion but does not lower storage cost. Copying to another Region does not reduce the storage price. Creating and deregistering AMIs does not change how the snapshots are stored or billed.

question: An operations engineer accidentally deleted several EBS snapshots that were needed for recovery. The company wants to be able to recover snapshots that are deleted by mistake for up to 30 days, without changing its existing backup scripts. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Create a Recycle Bin retention rule for EBS snapshots with a 30-day retention period
Enable termination protection on the instances that own the volumes
Configure an S3 Lifecycle rule on the bucket that stores the EBS snapshots
Enable EBS encryption by default in the Region
explanation: Recycle Bin retention rules keep deleted EBS snapshots and AMIs for a specified period so they can be restored, and they apply without changing the scripts that delete snapshots. Encryption by default does not prevent deletion. Termination protection protects instances, not snapshots. EBS snapshots are stored in AWS-managed storage that is not exposed as a customer S3 bucket, so S3 Lifecycle rules cannot apply.

question: A company requires that all EBS data be encrypted with AWS KMS and is reviewing how EBS encryption works. Which statements about EBS encryption are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Only Provisioned IOPS SSD volume types support encryption
Encryption must be implemented inside the guest operating system because EBS has no native encryption
Data moving between an encrypted volume and the EC2 instance it is attached to is encrypted
An unencrypted volume can be encrypted in place by modifying a volume attribute
Snapshots created from an encrypted volume are automatically encrypted
explanation: EBS encryption protects data at rest on the volume, data in transit between the instance and the volume, all snapshots created from the volume, and all volumes created from those snapshots. An existing unencrypted volume cannot be encrypted in place; an encrypted copy must be created through a snapshot. EBS encryption is native, handled by AWS on the host with KMS keys, and supported by all current EBS volume types.

question: A security team requires that every new EBS volume and snapshot copy created in an AWS account is encrypted, even if a developer forgets to select encryption when launching an instance. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an AWS Config rule that deletes unencrypted volumes every hour
Require developers to use a launch template that specifies an encrypted root volume
Install a disk encryption agent in every AMI that the company uses
Enable EBS encryption by default in each AWS Region that the account uses
explanation: EBS encryption by default is a per-Region account setting that forces all newly created volumes and snapshot copies to be encrypted with the default or a specified KMS key, with no change to launch workflows. A Config rule that deletes volumes is reactive and disruptive. Launch templates can be bypassed. Operating system encryption agents add management overhead and do not encrypt snapshots natively.

question: A company wants to share an encrypted EBS snapshot with a partner AWS account so that the partner can create volumes from it. The snapshot is currently encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/ebs. What must the company do?
options: Make the snapshot public and give the partner the snapshot ID
Copy the snapshot and re-encrypt it with a customer managed KMS key, allow the partner account in the key policy, and share the copied snapshot
Export the snapshot to an S3 bucket and add a bucket policy that grants the partner account read access
Modify the snapshot permissions to add the partner account ID, after which the partner can use the aws/ebs key automatically
explanation: Snapshots encrypted with the AWS managed aws/ebs key cannot be shared because the policy of that key cannot be changed to allow other accounts. The company must copy the snapshot with a customer managed key, allow the partner account to use that key, and then share the copy. Encrypted snapshots cannot be made public, and EBS snapshots cannot be exported as objects to a customer S3 bucket.

question: A legacy licensing server runs on an EC2 instance, and its license is bound to the MAC address of the network interface. The company needs a warm standby instance in the same Availability Zone that can take over without re-issuing the license. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Create an AMI of the primary instance every night and launch it during failover
Place both instances behind a Network Load Balancer with health checks
Attach a secondary elastic network interface to the primary instance and move that interface to the standby instance during failover
Associate an Elastic IP address with the primary instance and reassociate it with the standby instance during failover
explanation: An elastic network interface keeps its MAC address, private IP addresses, and security groups when it is detached from one instance and attached to another in the same Availability Zone, so the license stays valid. An Elastic IP address moves only the public IPv4 address. An instance launched from an AMI gets a new primary interface with a different MAC address. A load balancer does not preserve a MAC address for the backend.

question: A partner allow-lists a single public IPv4 address for an EC2 instance that sends data to the partner. After the instance was stopped and started for maintenance, the partner began rejecting its traffic. How can the company prevent this issue in the future?
options: Enable termination protection on the instance
Assign a secondary private IPv4 address to the primary network interface
Enable the DNS hostnames attribute on the VPC
Allocate an Elastic IP address and associate it with the instance
explanation: An auto-assigned public IPv4 address is released when an instance stops and a new one is assigned when it starts, whereas an Elastic IP address stays allocated to the account and remains associated with the instance across stop and start. Termination protection does not affect addressing. A secondary private IP address is not reachable from the internet. DNS hostnames do not keep the public IPv4 address constant.

question: Two EC2 instances in the same VPC communicate with each other. The application is configured to use the other instance's public DNS hostname, and the finance team is concerned that this traffic is billed as internet data transfer. DNS resolution and DNS hostnames are enabled on the VPC, and the instances use the Amazon-provided DNS server. How is this traffic handled?
options: The public DNS hostname resolves to the public IPv4 address, so traffic leaves the VPC through the internet gateway
The traffic is dropped because security groups do not evaluate public IP addresses
The public DNS hostname resolves to the private IPv4 address from inside the VPC, so traffic stays on the private network
The traffic is routed through a NAT gateway and incurs NAT gateway processing charges
explanation: When the Amazon-provided DNS server is queried from within the VPC, an instance's public DNS hostname resolves to its private IPv4 address, so the traffic stays inside the VPC and is not internet data transfer. Resolution to the public address happens only for queries from outside the VPC. Security groups do not drop this traffic by design, and no NAT gateway is involved in traffic between instances in the same VPC.

question: A production database runs on a 500 GiB gp3 volume and is running out of space and IOPS. The company must grow the volume to 1 TiB and raise its IOPS to 8,000 without stopping the instance. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Modify the volume in place with Elastic Volumes to change its size and IOPS, and then extend the file system in the operating system
Attach a second 500 GiB gp3 volume and enable Multi-Attach
Change the instance to a larger type so that the volume's IOPS increase automatically
Stop the instance, detach the volume, and create a larger volume from a snapshot
explanation: Elastic Volumes lets you increase size, change IOPS and throughput, or change the volume type while the volume is attached and in use; afterward the partition and file system are extended in the operating system to use the new space. Restoring from a snapshot requires downtime. gp3 does not support Multi-Attach, and a second volume does not grow the existing file system. A larger instance can raise the instance's EBS limits but does not change the volume's provisioned IOPS.

question: A company wants to be able to launch its application servers in another AWS Region during a disaster. The servers are built from a custom AMI in us-east-1. What must the company do so that the AMI can be used in us-west-2?
options: Modify the AMI launch permissions to add the same account for us-west-2
Copy the AMI to us-west-2, which creates a new AMI with a new AMI ID in that Region
Create a snapshot of the AMI and attach the snapshot to an instance in us-west-2
Nothing, because AMIs are global resources that can be launched in any Region
explanation: AMIs are Regional resources, so they must be copied to the destination Region, where the copy receives a new AMI ID and its own copies of the backing snapshots. Launch permissions control which accounts can use an AMI in its own Region and do not move it across Regions. Snapshots cannot be attached to instances directly; they must be turned into volumes or AMIs in the destination Region.

question: A company builds a golden AMI in its tooling account. The AMI's snapshots are encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. A workload account in the same Region must launch instances from this AMI. Which steps are required? (Select TWO.)
options: Re-encrypt the snapshots with the AWS managed aws/ebs key before sharing
Remove encryption from the snapshots before sharing and enable it again in the workload account
Update the KMS key policy to allow the workload account to use the key for operations such as Decrypt and CreateGrant
Make the AMI public so that the workload account can find it
Modify the AMI launch permissions to share the AMI with the workload account
explanation: To share an AMI backed by encrypted snapshots, the owner adds the target account to the AMI launch permissions and grants that account permission to use the customer managed key, because the snapshots must be decrypted when volumes are created. AMIs encrypted with the AWS managed key cannot be shared, so re-encrypting with aws/ebs would block sharing. AMIs with encrypted snapshots cannot be made public, and snapshot encryption cannot simply be removed.

question: A company uses AWS Organizations with more than 200 accounts. The platform team publishes a new hardened AMI every week and must make it available only to accounts in the organization, including accounts that are created in the future. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Make the AMI public and instruct teams to filter by the platform account's owner ID
Add each account ID to the AMI launch permissions with a script that runs after every new account is created
Share the AMI with the organization ARN or with the relevant organizational unit ARNs
Copy the AMI into every account with a Lambda function that runs on an Amazon EventBridge schedule
explanation: AMI launch permissions can be granted to an organization or organizational unit, which automatically includes current and future member accounts. A public AMI exposes the image to everyone. Maintaining per-account permissions or copying the AMI into every account requires custom automation and produces many copies to manage.

question: A company deregistered several hundred old AMIs to reduce costs, but its monthly EBS charges did not decrease. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: Deregistered AMIs remain billable for 90 days before they are deleted
The EBS snapshots that backed the AMIs were not deleted and continue to incur storage charges
The AMIs were automatically moved to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier
Deregistration takes effect only after all instances launched from the AMIs are terminated
explanation: Deregistering an AMI does not delete the EBS snapshots that back it; the snapshots remain and continue to be billed until they are deleted separately. There is no 90-day billing period for deregistered AMIs, AMIs are not moved to the archive tier automatically, and deregistration takes effect immediately regardless of running instances.

question: A startup needs EC2 capacity for a 6-week proof of concept. Usage will be unpredictable, and the instances must not be interrupted while they run. The startup does not want any long-term commitment. Which purchasing option is MOST appropriate?
options: 3-year Standard Reserved Instances
A Compute Savings Plan with a 1-year term
Spot Instances
On-Demand Instances
explanation: On-Demand Instances require no commitment, are billed only for the time they run, and are not interrupted by AWS, which suits short and unpredictable workloads. Spot Instances can be interrupted when AWS needs the capacity back. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans require 1-year or 3-year commitments that a 6-week project cannot fully use.

question: A company wants to use Spot Instances to reduce EC2 costs. Which workloads are good candidates for Spot Instances? (Select TWO.)
options: A license server that must run continuously with a fixed IP address
A payment API that must remain available 24/7 without interruption
A CI/CD fleet that runs stateless build and test jobs that can be retried
The single primary instance of a self-managed relational database
A video transcoding queue in which each job is checkpointed and can restart on another instance
explanation: Spot Instances offer large discounts but can be interrupted with a two-minute warning, so they fit fault-tolerant, stateless, or checkpointed work such as CI builds and queue-based transcoding. A single primary database, a continuously required license server, and an always-on payment API cannot tolerate interruptions and should run on On-Demand capacity, ideally covered by Savings Plans or Reserved Instances.

question: A research company runs a large batch simulation on a Spot Fleet that requests only c5.4xlarge instances in a single Availability Zone with the lowest-price allocation strategy. The jobs are interrupted frequently. The company wants to reduce interruptions while keeping costs low. Which change should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Diversify across multiple instance types and Availability Zones and use the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy
Switch the fleet to On-Demand Instances in the same Availability Zone
Raise the maximum Spot price to equal the On-Demand price
Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the c5.4xlarge instances
explanation: Diversifying across instance types and Availability Zones gives the fleet more Spot capacity pools, and the price-capacity-optimized strategy chooses pools with the most available capacity at low prices, which reduces interruptions. On-Demand removes interruptions but costs much more. Raising the maximum price does not prevent interruptions that occur when AWS reclaims capacity. Reserved Instances are a commitment for steady workloads and do not fit a batch job designed around Spot pricing.

question: A company runs a queue-processing application on Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group. The company wants to minimize lost work when instances are reclaimed. Which actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
options: Associate Elastic IP addresses so that the instances keep their IP addresses after an interruption
Increase the EBS volume size so that more in-progress messages can be stored
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for EC2 Spot Instance interruption warnings that triggers checkpointing or graceful draining of the instance
Enable termination protection on all of the Spot Instances
Enable Capacity Rebalancing on the Auto Scaling group so that it launches replacements when it receives a rebalance recommendation
explanation: Spot interruption warnings give two minutes of notice through EventBridge and instance metadata, which can trigger checkpointing or a graceful shutdown. Capacity Rebalancing lets the Auto Scaling group proactively replace instances that are at elevated risk of interruption. Termination protection does not stop Spot interruptions, Elastic IP addresses do not preserve work, and larger EBS volumes do not prevent lost work.

question: A company has steady EC2 usage of about $20,000 per month. Over the next 3 years it plans to move some workloads from m5 instances to Graviton-based instances, shift part of the workload to AWS Fargate, and possibly move one application to another Region. Which pricing model provides savings while supporting these changes?
options: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the m5 family
Standard Reserved Instances for the m5 instances
Zonal Reserved Instances in the current Region
A Compute Savings Plan
explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply automatically to EC2 usage regardless of instance family, size, operating system, tenancy, or Region, and they also cover AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda. EC2 Instance Savings Plans are tied to one instance family in one Region. Standard and zonal Reserved Instances are tied to specific instance attributes and do not apply to Fargate or to another Region.

question: A company will run a large fleet of r6i instances in eu-west-1 for the next 3 years. Instance sizes and operating systems may change, but the company is confident that it will stay with the r6i family in that Region. The company wants the largest discount available from a Savings Plan. Which option should it choose?
options: A Compute Savings Plan with a 1-year term
An EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the r6i family in eu-west-1 with a 3-year term
On-Demand Capacity Reservations for the r6i instances
Spot Instances launched through a Spot Fleet
explanation: EC2 Instance Savings Plans provide the highest Savings Plan discount in exchange for committing to one instance family in one Region, while still allowing changes to size, operating system, and tenancy, and a 3-year term increases the discount. Compute Savings Plans are more flexible but give a smaller discount, and a 1-year term reduces savings further. Capacity Reservations provide no discount by themselves, and Spot is unsuitable for a steady long-running fleet.

question: A company plans to buy Reserved Instances for a steady workload. Management wants the largest Reserved Instance discount but also wants the option to recover part of the cost by selling the reservations if the workload is retired early. Which option meets these requirements?
options: Standard Reserved Instances, because they can be sold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace
Convertible Reserved Instances, because they can be exchanged for other instance types
A Compute Savings Plan, because it can be cancelled with 30 days of notice
On-Demand Capacity Reservations, because they can be cancelled at any time
explanation: Standard Reserved Instances provide a larger discount than Convertible Reserved Instances and can be listed on the Reserved Instance Marketplace if they are no longer needed. Convertible Reserved Instances can be exchanged but cannot be sold on the Marketplace. Savings Plans cannot be resold or cancelled on notice; only a small, recently purchased plan can be returned within 7 days of purchase. Capacity Reservations can be cancelled but provide no billing discount by themselves.

question: A retailer expects a large traffic spike during a 3-day sales event next month and must be certain that 200 m6i.2xlarge instances will be available in a specific Availability Zone during the event. The company does not want a long-term commitment. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Request Spot Instances with a maximum price equal to the On-Demand price
Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the m6i family
Create On-Demand Capacity Reservations for the instances in that Availability Zone for the duration of the event
Purchase 1-year zonal Reserved Instances for 200 instances
explanation: On-Demand Capacity Reservations reserve capacity for a specific instance type in a specific Availability Zone for any duration with no long-term commitment, and they can be cancelled after the event. Zonal Reserved Instances reserve capacity but require a 1-year or 3-year term. Spot Instances provide no capacity guarantee. Savings Plans give a billing discount but do not reserve capacity.

question: A company wants to migrate Windows Server and SQL Server workloads to EC2 and bring its existing licenses, which are licensed per physical core and per socket and are not eligible for License Mobility. The company must also track license usage to stay compliant. Which actions should a solutions architect recommend? (Select TWO.)
options: Launch the instances on EC2 Dedicated Hosts so that the company has visibility into sockets and physical cores
Launch the instances as Dedicated Instances, which expose socket and core counts for licensing
Use AWS License Manager to define licensing rules and track license consumption
Use AWS Compute Optimizer to enforce license limits
Use Spot Instances launched from a license-included Windows AMI
explanation: Dedicated Hosts give visibility into and control over the physical server, including sockets and cores, which server-bound BYOL licenses require, and AWS License Manager tracks and enforces license usage, including on Dedicated Hosts. Dedicated Instances run on single-tenant hardware but do not expose socket or core details or support host affinity. License-included Spot Instances do not use the company's own licenses. Compute Optimizer provides right-sizing recommendations, not license enforcement.

question: A healthcare company's compliance policy states that its EC2 instances must run on hardware that is not shared with any other AWS customer. The company has no software licenses tied to physical cores or sockets and wants to minimize management effort and cost. Which option meets these requirements?
options: Dedicated Hosts with host affinity and auto-placement configured
Dedicated Instances
Default tenancy instances in a cluster placement group
Default tenancy instances that process data inside a Nitro Enclave
explanation: Dedicated Instances run on hardware dedicated to a single customer, which satisfies the isolation requirement without allocating and managing individual hosts. Dedicated Hosts also provide isolation but add host capacity management and are mainly justified for socket- or core-based licensing or host-level control. Placement groups and Nitro Enclaves do not prevent other customers' instances from sharing the physical server.

question: An EBS-backed EC2 instance is failing its system status check because of a problem with the underlying host, while its instance status check passes. The company wants this kind of failure to be fixed automatically in the future, and the instance must keep its instance ID, private IP address, and Elastic IP address. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Enable termination protection and stop protection on the instance
Create a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_Instance with a reboot action
Create a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with the EC2 recover action
Place the instance in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum size of 1
explanation: System status check failures indicate problems with AWS infrastructure such as host hardware or power, and the recover action moves the instance to new hardware while keeping its instance ID, private IP addresses, Elastic IP addresses, and metadata. A reboot addresses operating system problems reported by the instance status check and does not move the instance off a failing host. An Auto Scaling group replaces the instance with a new instance ID. Termination and stop protection do not repair anything.

question: A CloudWatch alarm triggers the recover action for an EBS-backed EC2 instance after a system status check failure. Which characteristics of the instance are preserved after recovery completes? (Select THREE.)
options: Data held in memory at the time of the failure
Associated Elastic IP addresses
Data stored on instance store volumes
The private IPv4 address
The same physical host
The instance ID
explanation: A recovered instance keeps its instance ID, private IP addresses, Elastic IP addresses, and instance metadata, and its EBS volumes stay attached. Recovery restarts the instance on different hardware, so data in memory is lost and the instance no longer runs on the same physical host. Instance store data cannot move with the instance to new hardware.

question: A critical EC2 instance has termination protection enabled. An administrator logged in to the instance and ran the operating system shutdown command, after which the instance was terminated and its root volume was deleted. What explains this behavior?
options: The root volume had termination protection disabled at the volume level
Termination protection expires automatically after an instance has run for 30 days
Termination protection applies only to Spot Instances
The instance-initiated shutdown behavior was set to terminate, and termination protection does not block shutdowns initiated from the operating system
explanation: When the instance-initiated shutdown behavior is set to terminate, shutting down from inside the operating system terminates the instance, and termination protection does not prevent this because it only blocks termination requests made through the console, CLI, or API. The root volume was then deleted because DeleteOnTermination is true by default for root volumes. Termination protection is not limited to Spot Instances, is not a volume setting, and does not expire.

question: A company wants to prevent operators from accidentally stopping a critical EC2 instance through the console, the AWS CLI, or the API, while still allowing the instance to be rebooted. Which feature should be enabled?
options: Stop protection
Hibernation
Detailed monitoring
Termination protection
explanation: Stop protection blocks StopInstances requests from the console, CLI, and API until it is disabled, which prevents accidental stops while reboots remain possible. Termination protection only blocks termination. Hibernation is a way of stopping an instance while saving its memory, and detailed monitoring only changes the CloudWatch metric period.

question: A company currently scales its web application vertically by moving to larger EC2 instance types as traffic grows. The company wants to switch to horizontal scaling. Which statements about horizontal scaling are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Capacity is capped by the size of the largest available instance type
Session state should be moved off the instances, for example to Amazon ElastiCache or Amazon DynamoDB, so that any instance can serve any request
All instances must share a single EBS volume to scale out
A load balancer is typically used to distribute requests across the instances
Each scaling action requires stopping the instance so that its instance type can be changed
explanation: Horizontal scaling adds or removes instances, so applications should be stateless with sessions stored externally, and a load balancer spreads traffic across the instances. Stopping an instance to change its type and being capped by the largest instance size are characteristics of vertical scaling. Instances do not need a shared EBS volume to scale out.

question: An EBS-backed EC2 instance that runs a database needs more CPU and memory. The team decides to change the instance from m6i.large to m6i.2xlarge. What is required to make this change?
options: Terminate the instance and launch a new one, because instance types cannot be changed
Create a new EBS volume for the larger instance type and attach it
Stop the instance, change the instance type, and then start the instance
Change the instance type while the instance is running, and the change applies immediately
explanation: To resize an EBS-backed instance, it must be stopped, its instance type attribute changed, and the instance started again, which causes a short outage. The instance type cannot be changed while the instance is running. Termination is unnecessary because the EBS root volume persists through a stop. EBS volumes are not tied to instance types.

question: A security review found that a web application on EC2 is vulnerable to server-side request forgery (SSRF), which could allow an attacker to retrieve the instance's IAM role credentials from the instance metadata service. Which change will MOST effectively reduce this risk?
options: Move the instance to a private subnet behind a NAT gateway
Require IMDSv2 by setting HttpTokens to required on the instance
Enable termination protection and detailed monitoring on the instance
Remove the instance profile and store access keys in the application configuration file
explanation: IMDSv2 requires a session token obtained through a PUT request with a custom header before metadata can be read, which blocks most SSRF attacks that can only make simple GET requests. Long-lived access keys on the instance are less secure than temporary role credentials. A private subnet does not stop the application from being tricked into calling the metadata endpoint. Termination protection and monitoring do not affect metadata access.

question: A company with many AWS accounts in AWS Organizations must ensure that no one can launch an EC2 instance that allows IMDSv1, including administrators of member accounts. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Publish a launch template that requires IMDSv2 and ask all teams to use it
Use Amazon Inspector to scan instances for IMDSv1 usage every week
Create an AWS Config rule in each account that reports instances with IMDSv1 enabled
Attach a service control policy that denies ec2:RunInstances unless the ec2:MetadataHttpTokens condition key equals required
explanation: A service control policy applies to all principals in member accounts, including administrators, and denying RunInstances unless ec2:MetadataHttpTokens is required prevents IMDSv1-enabled instances from being launched. AWS Config and Amazon Inspector only detect the issue after launch. A launch template is optional and can be bypassed.

question: An application on EC2 loads a 40 GiB in-memory cache that takes 25 minutes to rebuild every time the instance starts. To save money, the company stops the instance every night and starts it every morning. The company wants the application to be ready faster in the morning. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Launch the instance with hibernation enabled and hibernate it at night instead of stopping it
Store the cache on an instance store volume so that it persists across stop and start
Reboot the instance at night instead of stopping it
Take an EBS snapshot every night and restore it every morning
explanation: Hibernation saves the contents of RAM to the encrypted EBS root volume and restores it when the instance starts, so processes and the in-memory cache resume without being rebuilt, and compute charges stop while the instance is hibernated. Instance store data is lost when an instance stops. Rebooting keeps the instance running and billed all night. Restoring a snapshot does not restore memory contents.

question: A solutions architect is preparing EC2 instances to use hibernation. Which requirements must be met? (Select TWO.)
options: The instance must be launched in a cluster placement group
The instance must use an instance store root volume
The instance must run on a Dedicated Host
Hibernation must be enabled when the instance is launched
The root volume must be an encrypted EBS volume with enough space to store the instance's RAM contents
explanation: Hibernation writes RAM to the EBS root volume, which must be encrypted and large enough to hold the memory contents, and hibernation must be enabled at launch because it cannot be turned on for an existing instance. Instance store root volumes are not supported. Placement groups and Dedicated Hosts are not requirements for hibernation.

question: A bank must keep certain customer data on premises in its own data center to meet data residency regulations, but it wants to run EC2 instances and EBS volumes with the same APIs, tools, and management experience as in an AWS Region. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: AWS Local Zones
AWS Wavelength Zones
AWS Outposts
EC2 Dedicated Hosts in the nearest AWS Region
explanation: AWS Outposts delivers AWS-managed racks or servers into the customer's own facility, so EC2 and EBS run on premises with the same APIs and console, keeping data local for residency requirements. Local Zones and Wavelength Zones are AWS-operated locations, not the customer's data center. Dedicated Hosts in a Region still store data in AWS facilities.

question: A gaming company is building a mobile multiplayer game that requires single-digit millisecond latency for players connected over 5G networks. Which AWS infrastructure option is designed for this use case?
options: AWS Local Zones
Amazon CloudFront edge locations
AWS Outposts
AWS Wavelength
explanation: AWS Wavelength embeds AWS compute and storage within telecommunications providers' 5G networks, so traffic from mobile devices reaches the application without leaving the carrier network, which gives ultra-low latency. Outposts runs in a customer's data center. Local Zones bring services close to metropolitan areas but not inside the 5G network. CloudFront edge locations cache content and do not host EC2 game servers.

question: A visual effects studio in Los Angeles has artist workstations that need single-digit millisecond latency to EC2 rendering instances. The closest AWS Region is too far away to provide this latency, and the studio does not want to host or manage AWS hardware in its own office. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Deploy the rendering instances in an AWS Local Zone in Los Angeles that is extended from the parent Region
Install AWS Outposts racks in the studio
Use Amazon CloudFront to accelerate the rendering traffic
Use AWS Global Accelerator to route traffic to the nearest Region
explanation: Local Zones place AWS compute, storage, and selected services in large metropolitan areas such as Los Angeles, giving single-digit millisecond latency to nearby users while AWS operates the infrastructure. Outposts would require hosting AWS hardware in the studio. CloudFront and Global Accelerator optimize the network path but cannot remove the distance to a Region that is too far away for interactive workstation latency.

question: A company wants AWS Compute Optimizer to produce right-sizing recommendations for its EC2 fleet that take memory utilization into account, so that it can safely downsize over-provisioned instances. Which actions should the company take? (Select TWO.)
options: Opt in to AWS Compute Optimizer for the account or the organization
Enable hibernation on all of the instances
Enable EBS encryption by default
Install and configure the CloudWatch agent on the instances to publish memory utilization metrics
Purchase a Compute Savings Plan
explanation: Compute Optimizer must be opted in, after which it analyzes CloudWatch metrics to recommend better instance types. EC2 does not collect memory utilization by default, so the CloudWatch agent must publish it for memory-aware recommendations. Encryption, hibernation, and Savings Plans do not supply utilization data for right-sizing.

question: An administrator lost the private key for an EBS-backed Amazon Linux 2023 instance. The instance has the EC2 Instance Connect package installed, and its security group allows SSH from the company network. Which methods can the administrator use to regain SSH access? (Select TWO.)
options: Retrieve the private key from the instance metadata service
Use EC2 Instance Connect with the required IAM permissions to push a temporary public key and connect
Download the private key again from the key pairs page of the EC2 console
Create a new key pair and associate it with the running instance through the ModifyInstanceAttribute API
Stop the instance, attach its root volume to a helper instance, add a new public key to authorized_keys, reattach the volume, and start the instance
explanation: EC2 Instance Connect lets an IAM-authorized user push a short-lived public key and connect without the original key, and editing authorized_keys by mounting the root volume on a helper instance restores access for EBS-backed instances. AWS does not keep a copy of private keys, so they cannot be downloaded again or read from instance metadata. A key pair cannot be swapped on a running instance through an API call.

question: A company terminates EC2 instances that run batch jobs when the jobs finish, but auditors require the root volume of each instance to be kept for later investigation. Currently the root volumes are deleted when the instances terminate. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Enable termination protection on the instances
Set the DeleteOnTermination attribute of the root volume to false
Enable stop protection on the instances
Enable Multi-Attach on the root volumes
explanation: By default the root EBS volume has DeleteOnTermination set to true, so it is deleted when the instance terminates; setting the attribute to false keeps the volume after termination. Termination protection would block the batch instances from being terminated at all. Stop protection only blocks stops. Multi-Attach shares a volume between instances and does not control deletion on termination.

question: A company discovers that a 500 GiB data volume attached to a production EC2 instance was created unencrypted before the company enabled EBS encryption by default. Compliance now requires this data to be encrypted at rest with a customer managed AWS KMS key. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Create a snapshot of the volume, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled and the customer managed key specified, create a new volume from the encrypted copy, and replace the original volume with it
Use Elastic Volumes to modify the Encrypted attribute of the volume while it remains attached to the instance
Change the default KMS key for EBS encryption by default to the customer managed key so that existing volumes are re-encrypted automatically
Create an AMI of the instance and turn on encryption in the AMI launch permissions before relaunching the instance
explanation: An existing unencrypted volume cannot be encrypted in place, so the supported path is to snapshot it, create an encrypted copy of the snapshot (or an encrypted volume from it) with the chosen KMS key, and swap in the new volume. Elastic Volumes changes size, type, and performance, not encryption. Encryption by default and its default key apply only to newly created volumes and snapshot copies and have no effect on existing volumes. AMI launch permissions control sharing, not encryption.

question: A company encrypts its EBS volumes in eu-west-1 with a single-Region customer managed KMS key. For disaster recovery, daily snapshots must be copied to eu-central-1 and must be restorable there even if eu-west-1 is completely unavailable. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Copy the snapshots to eu-central-1 and keep them encrypted with the eu-west-1 key, which EBS calls across Regions during a restore
Copy the snapshots to eu-central-1 and specify a KMS key that exists in eu-central-1 to encrypt the copies
Decrypt the snapshots before copying them, then enable EBS encryption by default in eu-central-1 so that restored volumes are encrypted
Share the snapshots with a second account and grant that account access to the eu-west-1 key in the key policy
explanation: When an encrypted snapshot is copied to another Region, the copy is encrypted with a KMS key that you specify in the destination Region (or the default EBS key there), so restores in eu-central-1 depend only on KMS in eu-central-1. A single-Region key cannot be used from another Region, so relying on the eu-west-1 key would fail during a Regional outage. Snapshots cannot be decrypted in place, and copies of encrypted snapshots are always encrypted. Sharing with another account does not move the data to another Region. Note that the first cross-Region copy is a full copy, which adds storage cost.

question: A brokerage must retain EBS snapshots of its trading database for 7 years in a write-once-read-many (WORM) state to satisfy regulators. After the retention is set, no user, including administrators with full IAM permissions, may delete the snapshots or shorten the retention period. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create a Recycle Bin retention rule for EBS snapshots with the maximum retention period
Attach an IAM policy that denies ec2:DeleteSnapshot to every user and role in the account
Lock the snapshots with EBS snapshot lock in compliance mode for the required duration
Lock the snapshots with EBS snapshot lock in governance mode for the required duration
explanation: In compliance mode, once any cooling-off period ends, a locked snapshot cannot be unlocked or deleted and its lock duration can only be increased, regardless of IAM permissions, which provides WORM retention. Governance mode allows users with the right permissions to unlock the snapshot or change the lock. An IAM deny policy can be removed by an administrator. Recycle Bin only keeps snapshots for a limited time after they are deleted and does not prevent deletion.

question: A security team must make sure that nobody in a production account can share EBS snapshots or AMIs publicly, and any snapshots that were already shared publicly by mistake must stop being publicly accessible. Private sharing with specific partner accounts must keep working. Which actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
options: Create Recycle Bin retention rules for EBS snapshots and AMIs
Enable block public access for EBS snapshots in block all sharing mode in each Region that the account uses
Lock all snapshots with EBS snapshot lock in governance mode
Create an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy that copies snapshots to a separate backup account
Enable block public access for AMIs in each Region that the account uses
explanation: Block public access for snapshots in block all sharing mode prevents new public sharing and makes already public snapshots private, while still allowing private sharing; it is a Regional, account-level setting. It does not stop public sharing of EBS-backed AMIs, so block public access for AMIs must also be enabled in each Region (existing public AMIs stay public and must be made private separately). Recycle Bin, snapshot lock, and Data Lifecycle Manager copies protect against deletion or loss, not against public sharing.
subtopic: Block public access for snapshots and AMIs

question: A company wants users in all of its AWS accounts to be able to discover and launch only AMIs published by Amazon or by the company's central image account. AMIs from any other publisher must not appear in the EC2 console or in API results. The company wants to preview the impact on existing workloads before enforcing the control, and it must apply the control across all accounts and Regions in its organization. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Enable block public access for AMIs in every account and Region by using a declarative policy
Deploy the approved-amis-by-id AWS Config rule to every account by using a conformance pack
Share the approved AMIs with the organization and remove launch permissions from all other public AMIs
Configure Allowed AMIs criteria that allow the amazon alias and the image account ID, start in audit mode, and then enable the setting across accounts and Regions with a declarative policy
explanation: Allowed AMIs limits which public or shared AMIs are discoverable and usable in an account based on criteria such as AMI providers, offers an audit mode to preview which AMIs would be affected, and can be applied across accounts and Regions through an AWS Organizations declarative policy. Block public access for AMIs only stops the account from making its own AMIs public. An AWS Config rule detects noncompliant instances after launch but does not hide AMIs. A company cannot change the launch permissions of AMIs that other publishers own.

question: A company recently required IMDSv2 on all EC2 instances. Since then, applications that run in Docker containers on the instances can no longer obtain the instance role credentials, and their AWS SDK calls time out. Applications that run directly on the host operating system still work. Which change will resolve the issue while keeping IMDSv2 required?
options: Increase the instance metadata PUT response hop limit to 2
Set HttpTokens to optional on the instances that run containers
Pass the instance role to each container through the instance user data
Add an outbound security group rule that allows traffic to 169.254.169.254
explanation: With IMDSv2, the response to the token PUT request is limited by the hop limit, and traffic from a container counts as an additional network hop, so with the default hop limit of 1 the containers never receive a token; raising the hop limit to 2 fixes this while IMDSv2 stays required. Setting HttpTokens to optional re-enables IMDSv1 and weakens SSRF protection. User data cannot attach a role to a container. The failure is caused by the hop limit, not by a security group rule.

question: A company is moving an application to Amazon EC2. Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which tasks are the company's responsibility? (Select TWO.)
options: Installing updates and security patches for the guest operating system on the instances
Patching the hypervisor that runs on the underlying hosts
Maintaining the physical security of the data centers that house the hosts
Configuring the security groups that are attached to the instances
Replacing failed hardware components in the physical hosts
explanation: Amazon EC2 is infrastructure as a service, so the customer manages the guest operating system, including updates and security patches, any application software, and the configuration of security groups. AWS operates the host operating system and virtualization layer and is responsible for the physical facilities and hardware.

question: A company has enabled EBS encryption by default, and new volumes are encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/ebs. A new policy requires all new volumes to be encrypted with a customer managed KMS key whose key policy is controlled by the security team, without asking developers to change their launch templates. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Edit the key policy of the aws/ebs key so that only the security team can administer it
Change the default encryption key for EBS encryption by default in each Region to the customer managed key
Disable encryption by default and require developers to select the customer managed key for every volume
Re-encrypt every existing volume in place with the customer managed key
explanation: EBS encryption by default uses a per-Region default key that can be changed from aws/ebs to a customer managed key, after which new volumes are encrypted with that key without any change to launch templates. AWS managed keys are controlled by AWS, so their key policies are not customer editable. Disabling encryption by default relies on every developer choosing the right key. The KMS key of an existing encrypted volume cannot be changed in place; a new key can be applied only through a snapshot copy.

question: A company takes a daily snapshot of a 2 TiB EBS volume and has kept every snapshot for two years. To reduce costs, an engineer proposes deleting all snapshots older than 30 days. A team lead worries that the remaining snapshots will be unusable because snapshots are incremental. Which statement is correct?
options: The oldest snapshot holds the full copy of the volume, so it must always be kept for later snapshots to be restorable
Deleting an older snapshot also deletes every later snapshot that references its data
Each remaining snapshot can still restore the complete volume, because data that later snapshots reference is retained when an earlier snapshot is deleted
The snapshots must first be converted to full snapshots by enabling Fast Snapshot Restore before older snapshots can be deleted
explanation: EBS snapshot deletion removes only data referenced exclusively by the deleted snapshot; data still referenced by later snapshots is preserved, so only the most recent snapshot is needed to create a full volume. Deleting older snapshots never deletes later snapshots, and there is no need to keep the first snapshot. Fast Snapshot Restore only speeds up volume initialization. Because referenced data is kept, savings may be smaller than expected.

question: A company runs a stateful application on EC2 instances that each have a root volume and three data volumes. For disaster recovery, the company needs a launchable image of each instance tagged dr=true every 12 hours, copies of those images in a second Region, and automatic removal of images and their snapshots after 7 days in both Regions. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: An Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager EBS snapshot policy that targets only the data volumes and enables cross-Region copy
A Recycle Bin retention rule for AMIs with a 7-day retention period in both Regions
An EC2 Image Builder pipeline that rebuilds the server from a recipe every 12 hours
An Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager EBS-backed AMI policy that targets the dr=true tag, with 7-day age-based retention and a cross-Region copy rule
explanation: A Data Lifecycle Manager AMI policy creates AMIs of tagged instances, including all attached volumes, on a schedule, copies them to up to three other Regions with their own retention, and deregisters expired AMIs while deleting their backing snapshots. A snapshot policy for data volumes does not produce a launchable image. Image Builder builds new images from a recipe and does not capture the running state of the application. Recycle Bin keeps deleted resources and does not create or copy images.

question: A research team runs a long simulation on a Spot Instance and writes checkpoints to the instance's EBS root volume. If the instance is interrupted, the team wants the same instance and its EBS volume to be preserved so that the job resumes automatically on that instance when Spot capacity returns. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: Use a persistent Spot Instance request with the interruption behavior set to stop
Use a one-time Spot Instance request with the interruption behavior set to terminate and DeleteOnTermination set to false
Enable termination protection on the Spot Instance
Use a Spot Fleet with the request type set to request and the lowest-price allocation strategy
explanation: Setting the Spot interruption behavior to stop keeps the instance and its EBS volumes, and with a persistent request Amazon EC2 restarts the stopped instance when capacity is available for the same instance type and Availability Zone; only EBS storage is billed while it is stopped. The stop behavior requires a persistent request, or the maintain type for a fleet, so a one-time request or a fleet of type request does not qualify. Terminating creates a new instance on relaunch, and termination protection does not prevent Spot interruptions.

question: A company plans to use an EBS volume with Multi-Attach enabled to give a clustered application on several EC2 instances shared block storage. Which statements about this design are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The volume can be a gp3 volume as long as all of the instances are built on the Nitro System
The instances can be spread across multiple Availability Zones to increase availability
The application should use a cluster-aware file system, because standard file systems such as XFS and EXT4 are not designed for simultaneous access from multiple instances
The Multi-Attach volume can also be used as the boot volume of each instance
An issue at the EBS infrastructure layer makes the volume unavailable to all attached instances, so the volume remains a single point of failure
explanation: Multi-Attach requires a clustered file system or application-level write coordination because standard file systems are not built for concurrent multi-host access, and an EBS infrastructure issue affects every attached instance, so the shared volume is still a single point of failure. Multi-Attach is supported only on io1 and io2 volumes, only for Nitro-based instances in the same Availability Zone (up to 16), and Multi-Attach volumes cannot be boot volumes.

question: A company runs a stateless application on Nitro-based EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Several times, an attached EBS volume stopped completing I/O while the instance still passed its system and instance status checks, and the application hung until an engineer replaced the instance manually. The company wants such instances to be detected and replaced automatically. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the VolumeQueueLength metric with an EC2 reboot action
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use attached EBS status checks, which report StatusCheckFailed_AttachedEBS, to mark impaired instances unhealthy and replace them
Create a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with the EC2 recover action
Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on the snapshots that the volumes are created from
explanation: Attached EBS status checks detect when EBS volumes attached to a Nitro-based instance are unreachable or cannot complete I/O, and an Auto Scaling group can be configured to use this check to replace the affected instance. The system status check passed in this scenario, so a recover action on StatusCheckFailed_System would not trigger. A queue length alarm with a reboot is an indirect signal and a reboot may not clear an EBS impairment. Fast Snapshot Restore only affects volume initialization after a restore.

question: A company runs several single-instance internal tools on EBS-backed, current-generation EC2 instances that have no instance store volumes. The company wants each instance to recover automatically from an underlying host hardware failure while keeping its instance ID and IP addresses, with no additional cost and without creating per-instance CloudWatch alarms. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Create a CloudWatch alarm for each instance on StatusCheckFailed_Instance with the reboot action
Place each instance in its own Auto Scaling group with a desired capacity of 1
Keep simplified automatic recovery, which is enabled by default on supported instances, turned on
Enable stop protection so that AWS migrates the instance instead of stopping it during a host failure
explanation: Simplified automatic recovery is enabled by default when supported instances are launched, costs nothing extra, and moves an instance to new hardware after a system status check failure while preserving its instance ID, IP addresses, and attached EBS volumes. A reboot action on the instance status check addresses operating system problems, not host failures. An Auto Scaling group replaces the instance with a new instance ID. Stop protection only blocks StopInstances requests.

question: A platform team deregisters AMIs frequently as part of image rotation. Twice this year, an AMI that production launch templates still referenced was deregistered by mistake. The team wants every EBS-backed AMI in the Region to be recoverable for 14 days after deregistration, except AMIs tagged lifecycle=temporary, which can be removed immediately. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Set a deprecation time of 14 days on every AMI
Create a tag-level Recycle Bin retention rule that targets AMIs tagged lifecycle=temporary
Copy every AMI to a second Region and delete the copies after 14 days
Create a Region-level Recycle Bin retention rule for EBS-backed AMIs with a 14-day retention period and an exclusion tag of lifecycle=temporary
explanation: A Region-level Recycle Bin retention rule applies to all resources of the chosen type in the Region, including untagged ones, and exclusion tags remove specific resources from protection, so deregistered AMIs can be restored for 14 days.
