A tag-level rule for the temporary tag would protect exactly the wrong AMIs. Deprecation only hides an AMI from default listings and does not stop deregistration. Copying to another Region adds cost and does not restore the original AMI ID.

question: A company runs an application on an EC2 instance with a single EBS data volume. The team assumes that AWS automatically backs up the volume so that it can be restored in another Availability Zone. Which statement about protecting this data is correct?
options: AWS does not automatically back up EBS volumes, so the company should create regular snapshots, which are replicated across all Availability Zones in the Region and can be restored to any of them
EBS volumes are synchronously replicated to a second Availability Zone, so no additional backup is required
EBS snapshots are stored in an S3 bucket in the customer's account, so S3 Cross-Region Replication protects them automatically
EBS volumes are automatically mirrored to instance store volumes, which survive an Availability Zone failure
explanation: AWS does not back up EBS volumes automatically; customers must take snapshots manually or with Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup. Snapshot data is replicated across all Availability Zones in the Region, so a volume can be restored in any AZ. An EBS volume is replicated only within its own Availability Zone. Snapshots are stored in S3 buckets that customers cannot access directly, so S3 replication features do not apply, and instance store is ephemeral host storage.

question: A company serves an already trained large language model for a customer support chatbot. It wants high inference throughput at the lowest cost per inference on Amazon EC2. Which instance family should a solutions architect recommend?
options: P5 instances with high-end NVIDIA GPUs that are typically used for large-scale model training
Inf2 instances powered by AWS Inferentia2 accelerators
Trn1 instances powered by AWS Trainium accelerators
X2idn memory-intensive instances without accelerators
explanation: Inf2 instances use AWS Inferentia2 chips that are purpose-built for deep learning inference, and AWS positions them as the lowest-cost EC2 option for generative AI inference. Trn1 instances use Trainium chips designed for training. P5 GPU instances are powerful but expensive for serving an already trained model. X2idn instances provide large memory but no ML accelerators.

question: A gaming company runs dedicated multiplayer game servers and an ad-serving engine. Both workloads are limited by CPU performance and need only modest memory and no local storage. Which EC2 instance family is the MOST appropriate?
options: Memory optimized (R family)
Storage optimized (I family)
Compute optimized (C family)
Burstable performance (T family) in standard credit mode
explanation: Compute optimized C instances are designed for compute-intensive applications such as dedicated gaming servers, ad server engines, batch processing, and high performance web servers. R instances add memory that these workloads do not need, and I instances add fast local storage. Burstable T instances in standard mode are throttled to their baseline once CPU credits run out, which suits low average utilization rather than sustained CPU load.

question: A 200 GiB gp2 volume hosts a small database. During a nightly batch, performance is good for about the first 30 minutes, and then I/O latency rises sharply. CloudWatch shows the BurstBalance metric dropping to zero and IOPS falling to about 600. The company wants a consistent 3,000 IOPS at the lowest cost, without downtime. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Increase the gp2 volume to 1,000 GiB so that its baseline performance reaches 3,000 IOPS
Change the volume to io2 with 3,000 provisioned IOPS
Take a snapshot of the volume and enable Fast Snapshot Restore on it
Use Elastic Volumes to change the volume type to gp3, which provides a baseline of 3,000 IOPS regardless of size
explanation: A gp2 volume earns a baseline of 3 IOPS per GiB, which is 600 IOPS at 200 GiB, and it can burst to 3,000 IOPS only while I/O credits last, as tracked by BurstBalance. gp3 includes a consistent 3,000 IOPS baseline independent of size at a lower price per GiB than gp2, and Elastic Volumes can change the type without detaching the volume. Growing gp2 to 1,000 GiB works but pays for five times the storage. io2 costs more for the same IOPS, and Fast Snapshot Restore only affects initialization of restored volumes.

question: A company runs a containerized batch platform on an EC2 Fleet that mixes On-Demand and Spot Instances. The fleet lists four instance types explicitly, which limits the Spot capacity it can use, and engineers must edit the configuration whenever AWS releases a new instance generation. Each node needs 8 to 16 vCPUs and at least 32 GiB of memory. Which change meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use attribute-based instance type selection and specify the vCPU and memory requirements in the fleet configuration
Add a launch template override for every current instance type that meets the requirements
Standardize on a single instance type and purchase a Compute Savings Plan for it
Switch the fleet to Dedicated Instances so that capacity is reserved for the platform
explanation: With attribute-based instance type selection, the fleet chooses any instance types that match the specified vCPU and memory ranges, which widens the set of Spot capacity pools and automatically includes newer instance generations as they are released. Maintaining an override per instance type is the manual approach the team wants to avoid. A single instance type reduces Spot flexibility, and Dedicated Instances change tenancy without reserving capacity.

question: An AI startup needs 16 GPU instances for a 10-day model fine-tuning run that starts in three weeks. The instances must be placed close together with low-latency networking, the capacity must be guaranteed for the whole run, and the startup does not want a 1-year commitment. Which option meets these requirements?
options: Spot Instances requested through a Spot Fleet with the capacity-optimized allocation strategy
Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML reserved for the required dates
A 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the GPU instance family
Regional Reserved Instances for the GPU instance type
explanation: Capacity Blocks for ML reserve GPU-based instances for a future start date, up to eight weeks ahead, for short durations such as days or weeks, and the instances are placed close together in EC2 UltraClusters for low-latency networking. Spot Instances provide no capacity guarantee and can be interrupted. Savings Plans and Reserved Instances require 1-year or 3-year commitments, and neither Savings Plans nor regional Reserved Instances reserve capacity.

question: An engineer increased the provisioned IOPS of an attached io2 volume 20 minutes ago, and the volume modification is still in progress. Load tests now show that the volume also needs more capacity, but the engineer's request to increase the volume size is rejected. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: io2 volumes do not support size increases while they are attached to an instance
The instance must be stopped before a volume can be modified a second time
A new modification can be requested only after the previous modification of the volume reaches the completed state
The size and the IOPS of a volume cannot both be changed within the same calendar day
explanation: With Elastic Volumes, a new modification for a volume can be started only after the previous one has reached the completed state, and a volume can be modified up to four times in a rolling 24-hour period. io2 volumes can grow while attached, and supported instances do not need to be stopped. Size and IOPS can both be changed, either together or in successive completed modifications.

question: An engineering firm wants to run graphics-intensive 3D visualization and rendering applications on EC2 and stream them to remote designers. Which instance family is designed for this kind of workload?
options: Inf family powered by AWS Inferentia
Hpc family for high performance computing
R family for memory optimized workloads
G family for graphics-intensive workloads
explanation: In EC2 naming, the G series denotes graphics-intensive accelerated computing instances with GPUs suited to 3D visualization, rendering, and graphics streaming. Inf instances accelerate machine learning inference, Hpc instances target tightly coupled HPC simulations, and R instances add memory without GPUs.

question: A company runs a Linux-based Java web application on m6i instances. The application and all of its dependencies are available for both x86 and Arm architectures. The company wants to lower its compute cost without reducing performance and with minimal changes. Which option should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Move the application to comparable AWS Graviton-based instances, such as the M7g family
Move the application to EC2 Dedicated Hosts
Move the application to x86 instances with the n suffix for enhanced networking
Move the application to storage optimized I-family instances
explanation: AWS Graviton-based instances, identified by the g in names such as M7g, are built on Arm-based AWS processors and are positioned by AWS as offering the best price performance in EC2 at a lower cost than comparable x86 instances, so a workload that already runs on Arm can move with little effort. Dedicated Hosts increase cost. Network-optimized and storage optimized instances add capabilities that the application does not need.

question: An internal web application runs on a t3.large instance that is configured in standard credit mode. Its CPU utilization averages about 12% per day, but unpredictable spikes several times a day need full CPU for up to an hour, and users notice slowdowns when the CPU credits run out. Which option is the MOST cost-effective way to provide consistent performance?
options: Replace the instance with an m5.large fixed-performance instance
Switch the instance to unlimited mode, because surplus credits are charged only if average CPU utilization over 24 hours exceeds the baseline
Replace the instance with a t3.2xlarge instance in standard credit mode
Add a second t3.large instance in standard mode behind an Application Load Balancer
explanation: In unlimited mode, a burstable instance can keep bursting after its credits are exhausted, and additional charges apply only when its average CPU utilization over 24 hours exceeds the baseline, which is 30% for a t3.large; at about 12% average there is no extra charge. An m5.large has a higher hourly price for the same performance. A larger T instance or a second instance increases the hourly cost to buy headroom that unlimited mode provides at no extra charge here.

question: A company purchased 1-year Standard Reserved Instances with regional scope for m6i.xlarge Linux instances with default tenancy in us-east-1. Which statements about these Reserved Instances are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The discount applies to matching usage in any Availability Zone in us-east-1
The Reserved Instances reserve m6i.xlarge capacity in every Availability Zone in us-east-1
The Reserved Instances can be exchanged for r6i Reserved Instances at any time
The discount can apply to other sizes in the m6i family, such as m6i.2xlarge, through instance size flexibility
The discount also applies to m6i usage in us-west-2
explanation: Regional Reserved Instances apply their discount to matching usage in any Availability Zone of the Region and, for Linux with default tenancy, across sizes in the same instance family through instance size flexibility. Regional Reserved Instances do not reserve capacity; only zonal Reserved Instances do. Standard Reserved Instances cannot be exchanged (only Convertible Reserved Instances can), and Reserved Instances apply only in the Region where they were purchased.

question: A company runs a critical application on 40 c6i.4xlarge Linux instances in us-east-1a, and a Compute Savings Plan covers this usage. During a recent scaling event, replacement launches failed with insufficient capacity errors. The company needs assured capacity for the 40 instances in that Availability Zone for the next several months while still paying discounted rates. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Purchase 3-year zonal Reserved Instances for the 40 instances in addition to the Savings Plan
Convert the Compute Savings Plan to an EC2 Instance Savings Plan so that it reserves capacity
Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for 40 c6i.4xlarge instances in us-east-1a and keep the Savings Plan, which continues to apply to the reserved usage
Request Spot Instances with a maximum price equal to the On-Demand price
explanation: On-Demand Capacity Reservations reserve capacity in a specific Availability Zone with no term commitment, and although they give no discount on their own, they can be combined with Savings Plans or regional Reserved Instances to receive discounted rates. Savings Plans do not reserve capacity and cannot be converted. Adding 3-year zonal Reserved Instances creates an unnecessary long commitment on top of the existing plan. Spot Instances provide no capacity assurance.

question: Two years ago a company purchased 3-year Convertible Reserved Instances for c5 instances in eu-west-1. The company has since migrated the workload to Graviton-based c7g instances in the same Region. How can the company keep receiving a Reserved Instance discount for the new instances?
options: Sell the Convertible Reserved Instances on the Reserved Instance Marketplace and buy new Reserved Instances for c7g
Modify the Reserved Instances to move them to a different Region where c5 instances are still used
Cancel the Convertible Reserved Instances and request a prorated refund
Exchange the Convertible Reserved Instances for c7g Convertible Reserved Instances of equal or greater value
explanation: Convertible Reserved Instances can be exchanged for Convertible Reserved Instances with a different instance family, operating system, or tenancy, as long as the new reservation is of equal or greater value, paying any true-up cost; the end date stays the same. Convertible Reserved Instances cannot be sold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace, exchanges cannot move a reservation to another Region, and reservations cannot be cancelled for a refund.

question: A company hibernates a large development instance every evening and resumes it every morning to save money. Which statements describe how the company is billed while the instance is hibernated? (Select TWO.)
options: Instance usage is billed at a reduced hibernation rate of 10% of the On-Demand price
Storage for the attached EBS volumes, including the RAM contents saved on the root volume, is billed
No instance usage charges accrue while the hibernated instance is in the stopped state
Data transfer charges apply when the RAM contents are written to the EBS root volume
A per-GiB hourly hibernation fee applies to the amount of RAM saved
explanation: While a hibernated instance is in the stopped state, there are no instance usage charges, but the EBS volumes, including the space that stores the RAM contents, continue to be billed as storage. AWS does not charge data transfer for writing RAM to the root volume, and there is no reduced hibernation rate or separate hibernation fee.

question: A company's bill shows high charges for public IPv4 addresses. The account has 120 EC2 instances with auto-assigned public IPv4 addresses that are used only by administrators for SSH, and 25 Elastic IP addresses that are allocated but not associated with any resource. Which actions will reduce these charges? (Select TWO.)
options: Convert the auto-assigned public IPv4 addresses to Elastic IP addresses, which are free while associated with a running instance
Enable detailed monitoring so that idle public IPv4 addresses are released automatically
Release the Elastic IP addresses that are not associated with any resource
Launch the instances in a cluster placement group so that they share a single public IPv4 address
Remove the public IPv4 addresses from the instances and give administrators SSH access through an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint
explanation: AWS charges for every public IPv4 address, including addresses on running instances and Elastic IP addresses, whether associated or not, so releasing unused Elastic IP addresses and removing public addresses that are not needed reduces the bill. An EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint provides SSH to instances that have no public IP address. Converting to Elastic IP addresses does not avoid the charge, and detailed monitoring and placement groups have no effect on public IPv4 addressing.

question: A security software vendor wants to run its own type-1 hypervisor on Amazon EC2 to test its products. The hypervisor needs direct access to processor hardware virtualization features such as Intel VT, and the vendor's license terms require a non-virtualized environment. Which EC2 option meets these requirements?
options: Launch the largest virtualized size of a Nitro-based instance family, such as a 48xlarge size
Launch the instances on an EC2 Dedicated Host so that the vendor can see the sockets and physical cores
Launch a bare metal (metal) instance size of a Nitro-based family, which gives the operating system direct access to the host hardware
Run the hypervisor inside an AWS Nitro Enclave that is attached to a standard instance
explanation: Bare metal instances remove the virtualization layer and are intended for workloads that need low-level hardware features such as Intel VT, or that need a non-virtualized environment for licensing or support. Even the largest virtualized size still runs on the Nitro hypervisor. A Dedicated Host gives visibility of sockets and cores for licensing, but instances on it are still virtual machines. Nitro Enclaves are constrained, isolated environments for processing sensitive data and cannot host a hypervisor.

question: A bioinformatics team runs a Linux batch tool that is compiled only for Arm and is CPU bound. Each job writes about 300 GB of intermediate files that are deleted when the job ends, and the team wants that scratch space on fast local NVMe disks that are included in the instance price instead of on separate EBS volumes. Which instance type fits these requirements?
options: c7g.4xlarge
c7gd.4xlarge
c7gn.4xlarge
c7i.4xlarge
explanation: In EC2 instance type names, c is the compute optimized series, 7 is the generation, g means AWS Graviton (Arm) processors, and d means the type includes local instance store volumes, so c7gd provides Arm CPUs plus local NVMe storage at no extra charge. c7g is EBS-only, the n in c7gn means network and EBS optimized rather than local storage, and the i in c7i means Intel x86 processors, which cannot run an Arm-only build.

question: A company runs a licensing server in us-east-1a. For disaster recovery, the team pre-created a secondary elastic network interface on the server and planned to move it to a standby instance in us-east-1b if us-east-1a becomes unavailable. During a test, attaching the network interface to the standby instance fails. What is the cause, and what should the team do?
options: The standby instance must be stopped before a network interface can be attached; stop it, attach the interface, and start it again
Source/destination checking must be disabled on the network interface before it can move between instances
Only a primary network interface can move between instances; make the interface the primary interface of the server
A network interface belongs to a subnet in one Availability Zone; for cross-AZ failover, remap an Elastic IP address or use DNS failover or a load balancer
explanation: A network interface is created in a subnet, and subnets live in a single Availability Zone, so an interface can only be attached to instances in that same Availability Zone. Moving an interface is a same-AZ standby technique; failover to another Availability Zone needs a mechanism that can point to a new subnet, such as remapping an Elastic IP address, Route 53 failover, or a load balancer. Secondary interfaces can be attached to running instances, source/destination checking only matters for routing appliances, and the primary interface cannot be detached at all.

question: A company deploys a third-party firewall appliance on EC2 with two network interfaces: the primary interface in a management subnet and a secondary interface in a data subnet in the same Availability Zone. Which statements about this design are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Each network interface can have its own security groups, so management traffic and data traffic can be filtered with different rules
Security groups are applied to the instance as a whole, so both network interfaces always share the same rules
The primary network interface can be detached and attached to a replacement appliance to keep its management IP address
Each network interface automatically receives its own public IPv4 address when the instance is launched
The secondary interface keeps its private IP addresses and MAC address when it is moved to a replacement appliance in the same AZ
explanation: Security groups are an attribute of a network interface, so a multi-homed instance can apply different rules on each interface. A secondary interface carries its attributes, including private IP addresses, Elastic IP addresses, MAC address, and security groups, when it is detached and attached to another instance in the same Availability Zone. The primary network interface can never be detached from its instance. A public IPv4 address assigned at launch goes to the primary network interface, not to every interface.

question: A partner allow-listed the auto-assigned public IPv4 address of a company's EC2 instance. To make sure the address never changes, an engineer plans to associate an Elastic IP address with the instance so that the current public IPv4 address becomes static. What will happen when the engineer does this?
options: The current public IPv4 address is released back to the AWS pool and replaced by the Elastic IP address, so the partner must allow-list the new address
EC2 converts the current public IPv4 address into an Elastic IP address that stays allocated to the account until it is released
The instance keeps both addresses, and the original public IPv4 address becomes static while the Elastic IP address stays associated
The association fails, because an instance that received an auto-assigned public IPv4 address cannot use an Elastic IP address
explanation: When an Elastic IP address is associated with an instance that already has a public IPv4 address, that public address is released back to Amazon's pool and cannot be reused or converted into an Elastic IP address. From then on the Elastic IP address stays the same across stop and start, so the partner needs to update its allow list once. The association does not fail, and the instance does not keep the original auto-assigned address.

question: An administrator launched a Windows Server instance from an AWS Windows AMI and selected a key pair. The administrator now needs the initial password of the local Administrator account to connect over RDP. How is this password obtained?
options: Read it from the instance user data, where EC2 writes the generated password
Retrieve it from AWS Secrets Manager, where EC2 automatically stores a secret for each Windows instance
Use Get Windows password in the EC2 console and supply the private key of the key pair to decrypt the generated password
Query the instance metadata service from another instance in the same subnet
explanation: For Windows instances, EC2 generates the initial Administrator password and makes it available encrypted, and the administrator decrypts it with the private key (.pem file) of the key pair chosen at launch; the caller also needs permission for GetPasswordData. The password is not placed in user data or in Secrets Manager. The instance metadata service is reachable only from the instance itself through a link-local address.

question: A software vendor shares a hardened AMI with a customer's AWS account. The vendor sometimes deregisters older AMIs without notice, and the customer must be able to keep launching instances from this exact image for at least 3 years. What should the customer do?
options: Turn on deregistration protection for the shared AMI from the customer account
Create a Recycle Bin retention rule in the customer account that covers the shared AMI
Reference the shared AMI ID in a launch template, which keeps the AMI available while the template exists
Copy the shared AMI into the customer account, creating a new AMI that the customer owns and that is not affected if the source is deregistered
explanation: Copying an AMI that is shared with you creates a distinct target AMI with its own ID that your account owns, and deregistering the source AMI has no effect on the copy. The vendor must grant read access to the backing snapshots and, if they are encrypted, share the KMS key. Deregistration protection and Recycle Bin protect only AMIs that the account itself owns, and a launch template only stores an AMI ID, so launches fail once that AMI is deregistered.

question: A platform team deregisters an EBS-backed AMI from its account without selecting any additional options. Which statements describe the result? (Select THREE.)
options: Instances that were launched from the AMI are stopped automatically
Instances that were already launched from the AMI keep running and continue to be billed
New instances can no longer be launched from the AMI
The EBS snapshots that back the AMI are deleted together with the AMI
Copies of the AMI that were made in other Regions are also deregistered
The backing snapshots remain in the account and continue to incur storage charges
explanation: Deregistering an AMI only stops it from being used for new launches; instances already launched from it keep running and keep incurring charges. By default the backing snapshots are not deleted and continue to cost money, unless the option to delete associated snapshots is chosen or they are deleted afterward. A copied AMI is an independent AMI with its own ID, so deregistering the source does not affect copies in other Regions.

question: A central imaging account shares a golden AMI in us-east-1 with 30 workload accounts. For disaster recovery, the imaging team copies the AMI to us-west-2. Workload accounts can launch the AMI in us-east-1 but cannot find the copy in us-west-2. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: AMI copies stay private until the source AMI is deregistered
Launch permissions are not copied with the AMI, so the imaging team must share the new AMI in us-west-2 with the workload accounts
The copied AMI keeps the same AMI ID, so the workload accounts must search for it by name instead of by ID
A cross-Region AMI copy can be used only by the account that copied it, so each workload account must copy the AMI itself
explanation: AWS does not copy launch permissions from the source AMI to the new AMI, so the copy in us-west-2 is private to the imaging account until it is shared again. The copy has its own new AMI ID, and if its snapshots are encrypted, the KMS key used in us-west-2 must also allow the workload accounts. Copies can be shared like any other AMI, and they do not depend on the source being deregistered.

question: An engineer creates a golden AMI from a running EBS-backed instance. The instance has an EBS root volume, an attached EBS data volume, two NVMe instance store volumes that hold a warmed cache, and a user data script that sets its hostname at first boot. Which items will NOT be present on instances launched from the new AMI? (Select TWO.)
options: Packages installed on the EBS root volume
Files stored on the instance store volumes
Data stored on the attached EBS data volume
The user data script of the source instance
Configuration files edited on the root volume
explanation: An EBS-backed AMI is built from snapshots of the EBS volumes attached to the instance, so the contents of the root volume and the attached EBS data volume are included. Data on instance store volumes is not included in an EBS-backed AMI and is not present on instances launched from it. User data is an attribute of the instance, not of its disks, so it is not part of the AMI and must be supplied again at launch, for example in a launch template.

question: Four days ago, a company bought a 3-year Compute Savings Plan with an hourly commitment of $60, but it meant to buy a 1-year plan. It is still the same calendar month, and the company has not reached its return limit. What should the company do?
options: Return the Savings Plan, which is allowed for plans with an hourly commitment of $100 or less bought within the last 7 days in the same calendar month
List the Savings Plan on the Reserved Instance Marketplace and then buy the 1-year plan
Exchange the Savings Plan for a 1-year plan of equal or greater value, as is done with Convertible Reserved Instances
Cancel the Savings Plan with 30 days of notice, after which the remaining commitment is waived
explanation: A Savings Plan with an hourly commitment of $100 or less can be returned if it was bought within the last seven days and in the same calendar month, and any upfront payment is refunded in full. Savings Plans cannot be sold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace, cannot be exchanged like Convertible Reserved Instances, and cannot be cancelled with notice once the return window has passed.

question: A company owns 1-year Standard Reserved Instances with zonal scope for 10 m6i.xlarge Linux instances in us-east-1a. Eight months into the term, a network redesign moves the workload to us-east-1b. The company wants to keep both the billing discount and the capacity reservation without paying anything extra. What should the company do?
options: Exchange the Standard Reserved Instances for new Reserved Instances in us-east-1b
Sell the Reserved Instances on the Reserved Instance Marketplace and buy new ones in us-east-1b
Modify the Reserved Instances to change their Availability Zone to us-east-1b
Do nothing, because zonal Reserved Instances apply automatically to any Availability Zone in the Region
explanation: Both Standard and Convertible Reserved Instances can be modified at no charge to change the Availability Zone, the scope, or the size within the same family, and after the change the capacity reservation and discount apply in the new Availability Zone. Only Convertible Reserved Instances can be exchanged. Selling and rebuying adds cost and effort. Zonal Reserved Instances apply only in their own Availability Zone; regional ones apply anywhere in the Region but do not reserve capacity.

question: A compliance officer is reviewing a design that uses Dedicated Instances for a workload that must not share physical hardware with other customers. Which statement about Dedicated Instances is accurate?
options: They are isolated at the host level from instances of other AWS accounts, but they might share hardware with non-dedicated instances from the same account
They can share hardware with other accounts in the same AWS Organization, because those accounts are linked to a single payer account
They are guaranteed to return to the same physical host after a stop and start, which supports host-affinity licensing
Their attached EBS volumes are also placed on single-tenant storage hardware that is dedicated to the account
explanation: Dedicated Instances run on hardware dedicated to a single AWS account and are physically isolated from instances of every other account, even accounts under the same payer, but they might share hardware with non-dedicated instances from the same account. They offer no host affinity or placement control, so a stopped and started instance might move to another host; that requires Dedicated Hosts. EBS volumes attached to a Dedicated Instance do not run on single-tenant hardware.

question: Before a product launch, a company created an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for 20 c7i.2xlarge Linux instances in one Availability Zone. After the launch, only 12 matching instances still run, but the team left the reservation in place as free insurance. Finance now sees charges for capacity that nobody is using. Which statement explains the charges and the correct action?
options: Only the 12 running instances are charged; the reservation itself is free until it is fully used
The unused slots are charged only because no zonal Reserved Instance covers them, so buying zonal Reserved Instances will make them free
Capacity Reservations are charged only for their first 30 days, so the charges will stop automatically
Unused reserved capacity is billed at the On-Demand rate, so the company should reduce or cancel the reservation when the capacity is no longer needed
explanation: A Capacity Reservation is charged at the equivalent On-Demand rate whether or not instances run in it, so the 8 idle slots are billed as unused reservation. Savings Plans and regional Reserved Instance discounts can apply to Capacity Reservations, but zonal Reserved Instance discounts do not, so buying zonal Reserved Instances does not make the idle capacity free. Billing continues for as long as the reservation is provisioned, so the right action is to modify or cancel it.

question: An EC2 instance has termination protection (the DisableApiTermination attribute) enabled. Which events can still terminate the instance? (Select THREE.)
options: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling terminates the instance during a scale-in event because it belongs to an Auto Scaling group
An administrator chooses Terminate instance for it in the EC2 console
A script calls the TerminateInstances API for it with credentials that have full EC2 permissions
A user runs the operating system shutdown command while the instance-initiated shutdown behavior is set to terminate
AWS carries out a scheduled event that terminates the instance
An operator stops the instance from the console to change its instance type
explanation: Termination protection only blocks TerminateInstances requests made through the console, CLI, or API. It does not stop Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling from terminating the instance during scale-in or health replacement (use instance scale-in protection for scale-in), it does not stop a shutdown from inside the operating system when the shutdown behavior is terminate, and it does not stop AWS from carrying out a scheduled termination event. Stopping an instance is not a termination. Termination protection also cannot be enabled on Spot Instances.

question: After an engineer edited /etc/fstab and rebooted an EBS-backed Linux instance, the instance stopped responding. The system status check passes but the instance status check fails, and a CloudWatch alarm with the EC2 recover action on StatusCheckFailed_System never triggered. What should the team do?
options: Wait for AWS to repair the underlying host, because instance status check failures require AWS involvement
Fix the configuration inside the instance, for example through the EC2 Serial Console or by attaching the root volume to a rescue instance and correcting the file
Change the alarm to apply the recover action to StatusCheckFailed_Instance so that the instance is moved to new hardware
Stop and start the instance so that it moves to a new host, which repairs the file system configuration
explanation: An instance status check failure with a passing system status check points to a problem inside the instance, such as an incorrect startup configuration or a corrupted file system, which the customer must fix. The bad fstab entry travels with the EBS root volume, so recovery or a stop and start onto new hardware would boot into the same error. The recover action works with the system status check, which detects AWS infrastructure problems, and those are not the cause here.

question: A company receives an AWS Health notification that an EBS-backed EC2 instance running a stateful application has a scheduled instance-stop event in 10 days because of degraded host hardware. The company prefers to deal with it during its own maintenance window this weekend. What should a solutions architect do during the window?
options: Reboot the instance, which moves it to healthy hardware and clears the scheduled event
Create an AMI of the instance and wait for AWS to stop it on the scheduled date
Stop the instance and then start it, which migrates it to a new host
Change the instance type while it is running so that it is placed on new hardware
explanation: For an instance with an EBS root volume, stopping and starting it at a convenient time migrates it to a new host, which is how to handle a scheduled instance-stop event on your own schedule. A reboot is not the same as a stop and start, because the instance stays on the same host. Waiting for the scheduled stop gives up control of the timing, and the instance type can be changed only while the instance is stopped.

question: To lower costs, an engineer stops an m6i.large Linux instance and tries to change its instance type to m7g.large, but the change is rejected as incompatible. What is the reason, and how should the engineer move the workload?
options: m7g is an Arm-based Graviton type and the instance runs an x86_64 AMI, so the engineer must launch a new instance from an arm64 AMI and migrate the application
Instance types can be changed only within the same generation, so the engineer must first change to m6g.large and then to m7g.large
The instance must be running when its type is changed, so the engineer should start it and use Elastic Volumes to apply the change
All EBS volumes must be detached before the type can be changed to a lower-cost type, so the engineer should detach them and retry
explanation: Vertical scaling by changing the instance type works only between compatible types, and AMIs are specific to a processor architecture, so an x86_64 instance cannot be changed to an Arm-based Graviton type such as m7g. The workload must be moved to a new instance launched from an arm64 AMI. m6g is also Arm-based, so it would fail the same way. Instance types are changed while the instance is stopped, Elastic Volumes changes EBS volumes rather than instance types, and volumes stay attached during the change.

question: A company with a single AWS account wants every new EC2 instance in eu-west-1 to require IMDSv2 by default, with a hop limit of 2 for container hosts, even when teams launch instances from launch templates or AMIs that do not specify metadata options. Existing instances will be handled separately. Which solution requires the LEAST effort?
options: Enable EBS encryption by default in eu-west-1
Set the imds-support attribute to v2.0 on every AMI that the teams use
Deploy an AWS Config rule that reports instances on which IMDSv2 is not required
Set the account-level instance metadata defaults in eu-west-1 to require IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 2
explanation: Account-level instance metadata defaults are set per Region and apply to every new instance that does not override them at launch, so one setting makes IMDSv2 required with the chosen hop limit; existing instances are not changed. IMDSv2 can additionally be enforced so that launches that would allow IMDSv1 fail. Setting imds-support on each AMI must be repeated for every image and cannot be undone. A Config rule only detects noncompliance, and EBS encryption by default is unrelated to the metadata service.

question: A web server on EC2 runs third-party plugins as the local user www. A monitoring agent on the same instance runs as root and needs the instance role credentials from the instance metadata service. The security team wants to stop every process running as www from reaching the instance metadata service. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Add an outbound security group rule that denies traffic to 169.254.169.254
Add a network ACL rule that denies outbound traffic from the subnet to 169.254.169.254
Add a local firewall rule, such as an iptables owner match, that rejects traffic to 169.254.169.254 from processes running as www
Turn off the instance metadata service by setting HttpEndpoint to disabled
explanation: The instance metadata service is reached through a link-local address that is handled by the host, so security groups and network ACLs do not filter that traffic, and security groups cannot express deny rules anyway. A local firewall rule in the operating system can block specific users or allow only trusted users, which keeps the root agent working. Turning off the metadata service would also break the agent. Requiring IMDSv2 alone would not stop a local process from requesting a token.

question: A company wants to hibernate EC2 instances at night instead of stopping them. Every candidate instance uses an instance family that supports hibernation, is launched with hibernation enabled, uses a supported AMI, and has an encrypted gp3 root volume large enough to hold its RAM. Which instances will NOT be able to hibernate? (Select TWO.)
options: A Linux instance with 64 GiB of RAM that was launched from a persistent Spot Instance request
A Windows Server instance with 16 GiB of RAM
A Linux instance with 256 GiB of RAM
A standalone Linux instance with 32 GiB of RAM and an associated Elastic IP address
A Linux instance with 8 GiB of RAM that is a member of an Auto Scaling group
explanation: Linux instances must have less than 150 GiB of RAM to hibernate, so a 256 GiB instance cannot. Instances in an Auto Scaling group cannot be hibernated, and Auto Scaling would mark the stopped instance unhealthy and might replace it. Windows instances can hibernate with up to 16 GiB of RAM, Spot Instances can hibernate when the request is persistent, and an instance keeps its Elastic IP address while hibernated.

question: A developer hibernates a large EC2 development instance before leaving on a 3-month sabbatical and plans to resume exactly where the work stopped. The developer also plans to switch the instance to a smaller instance type while it is hibernated so that it costs less after the return. Which statement is correct?
options: Both plans work, because a hibernated instance is in the stopped state and can be modified and kept for any length of time
AWS does not support keeping an instance hibernated for more than 60 days, and a hibernated instance cannot be modified, for example by changing its instance type
The instance can stay hibernated indefinitely, but its saved RAM contents are moved to Amazon S3 after 30 days
The instance type can be changed while the instance is hibernated, but the instance is started automatically after 14 days
explanation: AWS does not support keeping an instance hibernated for more than 60 days; to keep it longer, the instance must be started and then stopped normally, which loses the saved memory state. Unlike a normally stopped instance, a hibernated instance cannot be modified, so changing its instance type is not possible while it is hibernated. The RAM contents stay on the encrypted EBS root volume, which keeps incurring storage charges.

question: A company runs 400 virtual machines on VMware vSphere in its data center and must exit the data center within 6 months. The workloads cannot be refactored or re-platformed, and the operations team wants to keep its VMware Cloud Foundation tools, licenses, IP addresses, and runbooks while running the environment inside the company's own Amazon VPC. Which AWS service meets these requirements?
options: Amazon Elastic VMware Service (Amazon EVS)
AWS Outposts racks installed in a colocation facility
AWS Application Migration Service to convert the virtual machines into native EC2 instances
Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts that run the existing virtual machine images directly
explanation: Amazon EVS deploys and runs a VMware Cloud Foundation environment on EC2 bare metal instances inside the customer's VPC, so VMware workloads move without changing IP addresses, retraining staff, or rewriting runbooks. Application Migration Service rehosts servers as native EC2 instances, which replaces the VMware tooling. Outposts keeps hardware on premises or in a colocation site rather than in an AWS Region, and Dedicated Hosts run EC2 instances, not a vSphere environment. VMware Cloud on AWS is no longer resold by AWS and is sold by Broadcom.

question: A solutions architect is choosing between EC2 instance store and Amazon EBS for several workloads. Which requirements mean that the data must be kept on EBS rather than on instance store? (Select TWO.)
options: The data must survive when the instance is stopped and started again
The data is a cache that can be rebuilt from a database at any time
The storage must be included in the instance price with no separate volume charge
The volume must be detachable so that it can be attached to a replacement instance
The data is scratch space for a batch job and is discarded after each run
explanation: Instance store data is lost when an instance is stopped, hibernated, or terminated, and an instance store volume cannot be detached from one instance and attached to another, so persistence across stop and start and the ability to move a volume both require EBS. Rebuildable caches and throwaway scratch space are good fits for instance store, which is included in the instance price at no additional charge.
